meta.tagline: Seven hills, Atlantic light and the smell of freshly baked pastéis — the city rebuilds itself from scratch every morning

pills: Eat at the counter, not at the table
Get to the miradouro before sunset

overview.intro: Lisbon is built on seven hills — you'll understand this the moment you step into the city. The cobblestones are slippery, the streets are steep, but at the top of every hill there's a view. The city has made peace with this difficulty: trams climb, elevators help with the ascent, and people walk slowly. The Atlantic light hits here in a colour found nowhere else — not yellow, not amber, exactly Lisbon light. Azulejo tiles on every corner, fado seeping through a doorway, a pastelaria on every neighbourhood street. This city doesn't tell you to hurry.

local_word.definition: The word Portuguese has exported to the world. A longing for the past, for something distant, for something that perhaps never existed. Melancholic but not painful — a sweet sadness. Fado is Lisbon's own traditional music genre — songs performed with guitar accompaniment, exploring themes of grief, longing and fate. Its emotional foundation is saudade. Lisbon itself carries a little saudade: old neighbourhoods facing the Tagus, faded tiles, traces of an old empire.

rules.title: Eat at the counter, not the table — same place, half the price
rules.description: In most pastelarias and cafés in Lisbon, eating and drinking at the counter costs less than sitting at a table — sometimes half the price. An espresso at the counter might be €0.80, at a table €1.50. The same rule applies to breakfast and light meals. Standing, quick, cheap: this is Lisbon's morning rhythm.

rules.title: Tram 28 is a tourist trap — use the alternatives
rules.description: Tram 28E runs a beautiful route but is now completely packed with tourists. Don't leave your pockets open and keep checking them. The crowds can be genuinely exhausting. Walk to Alfama or try tram 12E. Take the bus to Graça instead of 28E. The city's elevadores are a completely different story: Elevador da Bica, Elevador da Glória — these are still local and lovely.

rules.title: Bacalhau every day different — but always the same fish
rules.description: The Portuguese say they have 365 recipes for salt cod (bacalhau) — one for every day of the year. It's a legend but grounded in truth: bacalhau is at the heart of Portuguese cooking. When you see 'bacalhau' on a restaurant menu, look at how many versions they offer. Bacalhau à Brás — with egg, potato and olives — is the most classic and the right place to start.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: Red metro line to Baixa-Chiado ~25 min · no surcharge

quick_facts.label: Transport
quick_facts.value: Viva Viagem card — metro, bus, tram, ferry

quick_facts.label: Weather
quick_facts.sub: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov ideal · Jul–Aug hot but breezy · Dec–Feb wet

tip.label: Free Lisbon — the best things cost nothing
tip.text: Miradouros are free. The Tower of Belém is free from the outside. Walking through LX Factory is free. Wandering Alfama's streets is free. The courtyard of Mosteiro dos Jerónimos is free — the interior is ticketed. Many museums are free or discounted on Sundays. The Tagus River ferry to Cacilhas is just €1.30 — the city's most beautiful and cheapest view.

overview.title: Welcome to Lisbon

transport.intro: The metro is fast, trams are beautiful but slow, the ferry is scenic. And walking — in Lisbon, really walking is the most beautiful way to discover everything.

items.title: Airport → City
items.description: The red metro line (Aeroporto station) connects directly to Baixa-Chiado — about 25 minutes, no surcharge. Use your Viva Viagem card for a standard fare. Taxis and Uber are also available; 15-20 minutes to the centre, €10-15 depending on traffic. The metro is the most practical option: cheaper than a taxi, faster than a bus.

items.title: Metro — fast and reliable
items.description: 4 lines (blue, yellow, green, red), 56 stations. Single fare €1.80. With zapping (pre-loaded credit), each journey is €1.47. Runs from 6:30am to 1:00am. Viva Viagem card costs €0.50 — bought once and reloaded repeatedly. The airport, Baixa, Chiado, Marquês de Pombal and Oriente are all on the metro lines.

items.title: Trams and elevators
items.description: Tram 28E has a beautiful route but is not recommended due to tourist crowds and pickpocket risk. Tram 15E goes to Belém — more modern, less crowded, the better choice. The elevadores are a completely different experience: Elevador da Bica, Elevador da Glória and Elevador de Santa Justa — valid with the Viva Viagem card.

items.title: Tagus Ferry — the city's finest view
items.description: From Cais do Sodré pier to Cacilhas: just €1.30, 10 minutes. From the other side you see the Lisbon skyline, the Ponte 25 de Abril bridge and the Cristo Rei statue. Most beautiful at sunset.

items.title: Walking — and the reality of the hills
items.description: Lisbon has seven hills and they really are steep. Comfortable, non-slip shoes are essential — cobblestones become like an ice rink when wet. The centre is small: Baixa to Alfama on foot is 20 minutes, Chiado to Bairro Alto is 5 minutes. But budget time and breath for climbing to Graça or the heights of Alfama.

callout.label: Viva Viagem card — how to use it
callout.text: Available at any metro station for €0.50. You can load a single fare, a 24-hour pass (€6.80) or zapping credit. Zapping is the most flexible: load credit in advance and pay €1.47 per journey — valid on metro, bus, tram, elevator and the Cacilhas ferry. The card is valid for one year; keep it if you're coming back to Lisbon.

transport.title: Getting Around

stay.intro: Where you stay in Lisbon determines how many hills you'll climb. The centre is practical, Alfama characterful, Príncipe Real elegant.

local_word.definition: Viewpoint. Every hill in Lisbon has one or several — spots looking out over the city, the Tagus and the Atlantic light. The touristy ones are crowded, the local ones are quiet. Arrive 30-40 minutes before sunset: to find a good spot and to see the light at its finest. Get a beer, a pastel or something in hand, and sit.

items.name: Baixa / Chiado
items.description: The flat ground of the city. Baixa is busy with shopping streets and Praça do Comércio; Chiado right beside it is far more refined — bookshops, cafés, Livraria Bertrand. Close to the metro, trams and ferry. Walking distance to everything. Busy but the right choice if you want to be central.

items.name: Alfama
items.description: Lisbon's oldest neighbourhood, dating from the Moorish period. Narrow streets, azulejo-clad buildings, laundry hanging from windows, cats on every corner. São Jorge Castle at the top. Fado lives here — at night music seeps through doorways. Touristic but still a living neighbourhood. Steep and tiring — but something different at every step.

items.name: Príncipe Real
items.description: Elegant buildings, tree-lined squares, design shops and good restaurants. An organic market sets up at Praça do Príncipe Real on Sundays. Walking distance to Bairro Alto and Chiado. Lisbon's quietest and most refined neighbourhood.

items.name: Mouraria / Intendente
items.description: Just below Alfama, the neighbourhood where the Moors settled after being expelled from Lisbon. Multicultural, noisy, colourful — Portuguese, African and Asian communities here. Fado has its roots here too — the first voices rose in these streets. Intendente square comes alive at night. Not touristic; real Lisbon life flows through these neighbourhoods.

items.name: Belém
items.description: 6 kilometres from the centre, by tram 15E or train. The Jerónimos Monastery, Tower of Belém and Monument to the Discoveries are here. The original Pastéis de Belém is here — Rua de Belém 84-92, since 1837. The queue is long but moves fast. If you want to try them in the city centre, Manteigaria (Chiado) is at least as good. Try to plan a separate day for a museum visit.

stay.title: Where to Stay

best_time.intro: Lisbon can be visited year-round but is at its best when it's neither too cold nor too hot.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The best time
items.description: May and June are Lisbon's most beautiful months. Jacaranda trees burst into purple blossom in May — Avenida Fontes Pereira de Melo and Príncipe Real are the best places to start. The weather is mild, sunny but not overwhelming. In June, Festas de Santo António — the city's biggest festival, sardine grills, street music, processions.

callout.label: Festas de Santo António — the night of 12-13 June
callout.text: A festival in honour of Lisbon's patron saint Santo António. On the night of 12 June the city celebrates across every neighbourhood: street parties in Alfama, Mouraria and Graça, music and dancing. The crowds are real but the atmosphere is unmatched. Sardine sandwich €2-3, beer €1-2. The most authentic Lisbon night of the year.

items.subtitle: Spring · Jacaranda trees, mild weather, fewer crowds

items.label: Summer
items.name: Hot but breezy
items.description: July and August are the busiest months. Temperatures reach 30-35°C but the Atlantic breeze keeps it from feeling oppressive. Sardine season runs May to August. Museums are crowded, restaurants need bookings. For beaches, Cascais and Estoril are 40 minutes by train.

callout.label: Cascais and Estoril — leaving the city
callout.text: From Cais do Sodré by train to Cascais: 40 minutes — all the way along the coast with sea views. Cascais is small, elegant and quieter than Lisbon. Just beach, sea and fish restaurants. Ideal for a day trip. A separate ticket is required — the Viva Viagem card is not valid for this journey.

items.subtitle: Summer · Atlantic wind cuts the heat, sardines in season

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Quiet and beautiful
items.description: September and October are Lisbon's most comfortable period. The summer crowds have gone, the weather is still mild, museums and restaurants are quieter. In autumn the sun hits at a lower angle — the light is soft, shadows are long, everything turns golden. Photographers' favourite season. Rain begins from November.

callout.label: LX Factory — old factory, new spirit
callout.text: In Alcântara, under the Ponte 25 de Abril bridge. A 19th-century textile factory restored into bookshops, cafés, restaurants and studios. A market sets up on Sundays — Lisbon's most interesting weekend market. Take tram 15E or walk 25 minutes from Cais do Sodré.

items.subtitle: Autumn · Summer crowds gone, the city breathes

items.label: Winter
items.name: Wet but quiet
items.description: From December to February Lisbon is rainy but doesn't freeze. The least crowded, cheapest hotel prices, emptiest museums. The city is decorated with lights over Christmas. Fado evenings are at their best in winter — listening to fado on a cold, rainy night in a small venue carries a different meaning.

callout.label: A fado evening — where and how
callout.text: For real fado, choose the small tascas in Alfama or Mouraria. Large tourist fado restaurants are expensive and feel inauthentic. Book at small venues like Tasca do Chico, Mesa de Frades or Zé da Mouraria. Fado usually begins after 9pm. Stay quiet; applause only after the song ends.

items.subtitle: Winter · Rainy but the cheapest time

monthly_highlights.text: Santo António: the city's biggest night — grilled sardines in the streets, decorated neighbourhood parades, dancing till dawn.
Peak season: hot, crowded and alive; sightsee early and leave midday to the river breeze.
The ideal season: golden light, a sea still swimmable, shorter queues — Lisbon at its best.
São Martinho: 'magusto' day of chestnut smoke and jeropiga wine; the chestnut braziers smoulder on street corners.

best_time.title: When to Go

eat.intro: Lisbon is cheap and delicious — if you eat in the right places. Start at a pastelaria corner, move on to a tasca, finish with ginjinha.

local_word.definition: The Portuguese version of Spanish tapas — but simpler, more garlicky, more direct. Small plates, eaten while sharing. Classics: pastéis de bacalhau (salt cod fritters), amêijoas à Bulhão Pato (clams in garlic), peixinhos da horta (tempura green beans — a dish the Portuguese taught the Japanese). With a bottle of vinho verde alongside, the evening completes itself.

items.name: Pastel de nata
items.description: An egg custard tart invented by monastery monks. The top is caramelised and lightly scorched, the pastry layered and crisp. Dust with cinnamon and icing sugar. At the counter, standing, with an espresso. Manteigaria (Chiado): when the bell rings, they've just come out of the oven. Pastéis de Belém is the original — since 1837, in Belém — but Manteigaria is at least as good and right in the city centre.
items.tag: Manteigaria, Chiado · eat at the counter · early morning · €1.50

items.name: Bifana
items.description: Pork marinated in white wine, garlic and rosemary, stuffed into a papo seco roll. The bread absorbs the sauce — this is critical. If there's a yellow mustard bottle on the counter, that place knows what it's doing. As Bifanas do Afonso, Rua da Madalena 146 — standing, fast, cheap.
items.tag: As Bifanas do Afonso, Rua da Madalena 146 · eat standing · €2.50–3.50

items.name: Bacalhau à Brás
items.description: Salt cod, thin matchstick fries, egg, onion, olives and parsley — all cooked together in one pan. The result looks simple but the flavour is layered. Said to have been invented in the 19th century by a tavern owner in Bairro Alto. Start your bacalhau journey in Lisbon here — the most approachable, most classic version for first-timers.

items.name: Grilled sardines
items.description: Lisbon's seasonal dish from May to August. During the Santo António festival in June, the smell of grilled sardines fills every street corner — that smell is the scent of Lisbon's summer. With only lemon and bread. Fresh sardines are hard to find in winter; better not to order them in that season.

items.name: Ginjinha
items.description: Sour cherry liqueur, in a small glass, €1.50. Around 5pm there's a strange moment in Lisbon — lunch is over, evening hasn't arrived yet, nobody's hungry but everyone is stopping somewhere. This is exactly the moment for ginjinha. A Ginjinha has been at Largo de São Domingos since 1840 — go in, say what you want, take it, leave. A few doors along is Ginjinha Sem Rival. Try both; it takes ten minutes, the difference is yours to decide.
items.tag: A Ginjinha, Largo de São Domingos · €1.50 · since 1840

items.name: Tasca lunch
items.description: Small, family-run, usually no printed menu or written on a chalkboard. Ask for the prato do dia (dish of the day), they'll tell you what's available, you take it. Fish, meat, a little wine — €8-12 all in. These kind of tascas are still going strong in Mouraria and Intendente. Zé da Mouraria is legendary: lunch service only, cash preferred. Reservation essential.

callout.label: Time Out Market — how to use it
callout.text: At Cais do Sodré, on the river. Good for trying several things at once — but a nightmare if you go at the wrong time. Between 1-2pm and 7-9pm, finding a seat is impossible. Sit first, then choose your food. Around €20-25 per person. Some of the city's best chefs have stalls here.

eat.title: What to Eat

hidden_gems.intro: Lisbon's best places usually appear when you climb a staircase or turn into a narrow street.

items.name: Miradouro da Graça
items.description: Behind São Jorge Castle, in the Graça neighbourhood. Most tourists end up at Portas do Sol or Santa Luzia — Graça is less known, quieter, the view equally beautiful. Go in the early morning or before sunset. If you're going at sunset, don't forget to bring a beer. Sit, take a sip and enjoy the moment. In the view before you, the Tagus, Alfama and the whole city will be waiting.
items.rarity: The viewpoint Lisbonites go to, not the one tourists photograph

items.name: Livraria Bertrand
items.description: In Chiado, Rua Garrett 73. Open since 1732 — according to the Guinness Book of Records, the world's oldest bookshop still in operation. Small rooms, old wooden shelves, books in Portuguese and foreign languages. Even if you don't buy a book, go in, sit, stay a few minutes. You feel as though a whole history has settled over you.
items.rarity: Portugal's book paradise — Europe's oldest bookshop

items.name: Elevador da Bica
items.description: A steep funicular tram connecting the Bica neighbourhood to Cais do Sodré. Running since 1892. Not for the photograph — ride it because this is genuinely the way to travel this route. Your Viva Viagem card is valid here. At the bottom, walking distance to Mercado da Ribeira. At the top, get lost in Bica's narrow streets.
items.rarity: Lisbon by elevator — the descent of Bica

items.name: Conserveira de Lisboa
items.description: At the entrance to Alfama, Rua dos Bacalhoeiros 34. Open since 1930. Inside, dozens of sardine, tuna and octopus tins — in colourful cans with designs from another era. A wonderful option for putting memories in your suitcase before you leave or bringing gifts for loved ones, at reasonable prices.
items.rarity: Tinned fish — Lisbon's most beautiful souvenir shops

items.name: Cacilhas Ferry
items.description: From Cais do Sodré pier to Cacilhas: 10 minutes, €1.30. As the ferry moves, the Lisbon skyline, the Ponte 25 de Abril bridge and the Cristo Rei statue on the hill gradually come into sharper view. The finest view is during the crossing. Once you arrive in Cacilhas, you can eat fresh fish at the small restaurants on the waterfront while looking back at the city. Try to return at sunset — Lisbon takes on the most beautiful shade of orange at that hour.
items.rarity: Cross the Tagus and come back — Lisbon's skyline for €1.30

items.name: Calçada Portuguesa — Rossio Square
items.description: Portugal's distinctive handmade black-and-white cobblestone mosaic. The finest example is in Rossio Square: wave-like curves simulating the sea, every stone placed by hand. The Portuguese took this technique to Brazil too. That's why it's no coincidence that Rio de Janeiro's famous pavements show the same craftsmanship. To see the mosaic's full pattern you need to look from slightly above; from the balcony of a café at the edge of the square, or from nearby steps, the whole design reveals itself.
items.rarity: Portugal's history set into the pavement

callout.label: Feira da Ladra — Lisbon's oldest market
callout.text: Every Tuesday and Saturday, above Alfama at Campo de Santa Clara. The name means 'Thief's Market' — second-hand goods, antiques, records, books, jewellery. Tuesday mornings are quieter; Saturdays busier but more colourful. Prices accept haggling. Free entry. Miradouro da Graça is within walking distance — you can fit both into the same morning.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems

items.label: Eat a pastel de nata at the counter
items.sub: Manteigaria, in Chiado. When the bell rings, they've just come out of the oven. Cinnamon and icing sugar on top. Espresso alongside. €1.50.

items.label: Eat a bifana — standing, with mustard
items.sub: As Bifanas do Afonso, Rua da Madalena 146. If there's a yellow mustard bottle on the counter, you're in the right place. Eat standing, eat fast.

items.label: Take the Cacilhas ferry across
items.sub: Cais do Sodré pier. €1.30, 10 minutes. Lisbon's skyline ahead of you the whole way. Try to return at sunset.

items.label: Drink ginjinha — Largo de São Domingos
items.sub: A Ginjinha at Largo de São Domingos, since 1840. Go around 5pm, drink sour cherry liqueur from a small glass, €1.50. Ginjinha Sem Rival is a few doors along — try both.

items.label: Have lunch at a tasca
items.sub: Go into a small tasca in Mouraria or Intendente. Ask for the prato do dia (dish of the day), take whatever's available. €8-12 all in. Bring cash.

items.label: Go to Miradouro da Graça
items.sub: Graça neighbourhood, not touristy and quiet. Arrive at least 30 minutes before sunset — to find a good spot. When you sit, the Tagus, Alfama and the whole city spread out before you.

items.label: Get lost in Alfama's streets
items.sub: Go in without a map. Head upward through Alfama, stop somewhere, then come back down. Cats on every corner, fado seeping through doorways.

items.label: Ride the Elevador da Bica
items.sub: With your Viva Viagem card. From Bica neighbourhood to Cais do Sodré. Running since 1892.

items.label: Go into Conserveira de Lisboa
items.sub: Alfama entrance, Rua dos Bacalhoeiros 34. Small shop open since 1930. Colourful tins of sardines, tuna, octopus — high quality, fits in your suitcase, a great gift.

items.label: Go into Livraria Bertrand
items.sub: Rua Garrett 73, Chiado. Since 1732. The world's oldest bookshop still in operation.

items.label: Go to LX Factory
items.sub: Under the bridge in Alcântara, a restored old factory. Cafés, bookshops, shops. Sundays are its liveliest day. Take tram 15E.

items.label: Listen to fado — in a small venue
items.sub: Tasca do Chico and Mesa de Frades are small fado venues in Alfama. Starts after 9pm. Reservation essential. No applause until the song ends.

checklist.title: Lisbon Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Lisbon will pull you back. Next time, come slower.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Lisbon is a sweet city, but the tourism wave brought a few classic traps. Know these four and live the saudade for real.

items.name: Queueing for tram 28 at midday
items.description: The legendary tram is now a pickpocket bus at noon: an hour's queue, then a ride packed like sardines.
items.instead: Ride the same line before 8 am or try the 12E; better still, walk the route — Alfama exists to be walked.

items.name: Mistaking the couvert for a gift
items.description: The bread, olives and cheese that land on your table are not free; touch them and they're on the bill.
items.instead: If you don't want it, smile and send it back: 'não, obrigado' is enough — nobody minds, and the bill stays clean.

items.name: Haggling a tuk-tuk city tour
items.description: The hills are the excuse and the tariffs are wild; a half-hour tour can cost three times a taxi.
items.instead: The funiculars (Bica, Glória) and the tram's quiet hours handle the hills; if a tuk-tuk it must be, lock the price before boarding.

items.name: Hunting the nata only in the Belém queue
items.description: Pastéis de Belém is historic and lovely, but it isn't the only truth; an hour's queue is not required.
items.instead: Take a warm nata from the counter at Manteigaria, dust the cinnamon, be happy in thirty seconds; if you go to Belém, go at opening time.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: In Lisbon, avoid the place with a photo menu and a waiter at the door; enter the tasca with paper tablecloths and a handwritten menu. Half the price, twice the flavour, three times the story.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: Hills, nata and the far bank of the river

steps.title: Alfama morning
steps.description: Climb the narrow lanes: washing lines, azulejo façades, fado drifting from a corner. Coffee break at Miradouro da Graça.

steps.title: São Jorge Castle or the cathedral
steps.description: From the castle the city lies tile by tile at your feet; if the queue is long, the cathedral + the Portas do Sol view will do.

steps.title: Lunch at a tasca
steps.description: The fish of the day, a jug of vinho da casa; the bill surprisingly small, the satisfaction large.

steps.title: Chiado + Bica
steps.description: Browse Bertrand (the world's oldest bookshop), then descend the slopes beside the Bica funicular.

steps.title: Cacilhas ferry
steps.description: Cross the river and watch Lisbon at sunset from the far bank; the return ferry is the city's cheapest scenic cruise.

steps.title: Bairro Alto evening
steps.description: Tiny bars, glasses on the street, fado leaking from somewhere; the night here is best unplanned.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: Hills and river
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: Alfama, castle, Chiado, ferry.

steps.title: Belém and the discoveries
steps.description: Jerónimos Monastery in the morning (go early), Belém Tower and the Monument of Discoveries, MAAT in the afternoon; eat the nata here at the historic bakery.

steps.title: Sintra escape and goodbye
steps.description: Morning train to Sintra: Pena Palace + the well of Quinta da Regaleira, then an evening in Príncipe Real and one last ginjinha.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Portuguese is not Spanish — just knowing that wins hearts in Lisbon.

items.meaning: Good morning — until noon; after that, boa tarde
Thank you — ends in -o if you're male, -a if you're female
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — ginjinha glasses rise to this
See you soon — the warm goodbye Lisboetas use constantly
